title: “GREAT IS YOUR FAITHFULNESS” WAS WRITTEN WHILE JERUSALEM WAS IN RUINS
paragraphs: “GREAT IS YOUR FAITHFULNESS” WAS WRITTEN WHILE JERUSALEM WAS IN RUINS

Before these words became a song of comfort, they were a confession of faith rising from unbearable grief. And if your life feels like it is falling apart, the story behind Lamentations 3 may change how you understand the faithfulness of God forever.
There is something deeply unsettling about the words “Great is Your faithfulness.”
Not because they are difficult to believe when life is beautiful.
But because of where those words appear in Scripture.
They were not spoken from a palace overflowing with prosperity.
They were not written in the middle of a celebration, after every prayer had been answered and every enemy defeated.
They appear in a book filled with tears.
A book written in the shadow of Jerusalem's destruction.
A book where the streets are devastated, families are grieving, and the people of God are confronting the consequences of their rebellion.
And right there, surrounded by descriptions of suffering, we encounter one of the most breathtaking declarations in the entire Bible.
“Great is thy faithfulness.” — Lamentations 3:23 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not great is my understanding.
Not great is my strength.
Not great is my ability to hold everything together.
Great is Your faithfulness.
Because sometimes the most extraordinary confession of faith is not made by someone who has escaped the fire.
It is made by someone still standing in the ashes.
And perhaps that is why you need to hear this today.
Because there are people reading these words who know exactly what it means to live among ruins.
Your Jerusalem may not be a city destroyed by an invading army.
It may be a marriage that has become painfully distant.
A child you have prayed for until you no longer know what to say.
A diagnosis that changed the way you look at tomorrow.
A betrayal that shattered your ability to trust.
A financial struggle that has quietly stolen your sleep.
Or perhaps something even harder to explain.
You still go to church.
You still smile when people greet you.
You still tell everyone that God is good.
But when the house becomes quiet, and nobody is watching, you wonder why the God you love has allowed your life to become so painful.
And somewhere beneath all the prayers you know how to pray is a question you are almost afraid to ask.
Lord, are You still faithful when everything around me is falling apart?
That is not a modern question.
The book of Lamentations forces us to confront it.
In 586 BC, Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians. The temple was destroyed. The city was devastated. Many were killed, and others were carried into exile.
The place that had represented worship, national identity, and the visible presence of God's covenant promises lay in ruins.
And Scripture does not romanticize what happened.
Lamentations describes hunger, bereavement, humiliation, abandonment, and anguish so intense that the writer struggles to find language for it.
This was not simply an unfortunate historical tragedy.
The biblical prophets had repeatedly warned Judah that persistent idolatry, injustice, and covenant unfaithfulness would bring judgment.
God had not failed to keep His word.
Tragically, His warnings had proven true.
And that makes the declaration in Lamentations 3 even more astonishing.
Because God's faithfulness was not merely the promise that He would bless His people when they obeyed.
His faithfulness also meant that He would remain true to His holy character, even when His people rebelled.
The writer does not deny the devastation.
He does not pretend the suffering is imaginary.
He does not call judgment a blessing.
Instead, he looks directly into the darkness and remembers something the darkness cannot erase.
Listen to the movement of his heart:
“This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.”
— Lamentations 3:21 (KJV)
Notice what happens.
His circumstances have not suddenly changed.
Jerusalem has not been rebuilt.
The temple has not been restored.
The grief has not disappeared.
But something changes within him.
He remembers.
And what he remembers becomes the foundation of his hope.
“It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”
— Lamentations 3:22–23 (KJV)
Now we must look beneath the familiar English words, because the original Hebrew makes this confession even richer.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as “mercies” in verse 22 is חַסְדֵי (ḥasdei), from ḥesed (חֶסֶד).
It speaks of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, and faithful kindness.
Not merely a passing feeling of affection.
Not a momentary emotional response.
It describes love that acts faithfully according to God's character and covenant commitments.
The Hebrew word behind “compassions” is רַחֲמָיו (raḥamav), from raḥamim, a word associated with deep tenderness and mercy.
And the declaration “Great is thy faithfulness” comes from the Hebrew:
רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ
Rabbah emunatekha.
Literally, “Great is Your faithfulness.”
The word emunah (אֱמוּנָה) carries the sense of firmness, reliability, and faithfulness.
The writer is not saying that God has made his circumstances easy.
He is declaring that God's character remains trustworthy even when his circumstances are devastating.
And there is another detail we must not overlook.

The Hebrew text of Lamentations 3:22 contains a textual and translation question. Many traditional English translations, including the King James Version, read that God's mercies are why “we are not consumed.” Other translations render the verse along the lines that the LORD's steadfast love never ceases.
Both readings direct our attention toward the endurance of God's covenant mercy, but they should not be treated as identical word-for-word translations.
The central confession remains unmistakable.
God's compassion has not reached its end.
Even in judgment, His mercy has not vanished.
Even in national devastation, His covenant purposes have not been extinguished.
Even when His people have lost so much, God has not ceased to be God.
And perhaps this is where the words begin to reach into the places you have been trying to hide.
Because some of us have quietly built our understanding of God's faithfulness around the things He gives us.
When the job is secure, God is faithful.
When the family is healthy, God is faithful.
When the bills are paid, God is faithful.
When the prayer is answered the way we hoped, God is faithful.
But what happens when the job disappears?
When the relationship breaks?
When the test results are frightening?
When the prayer seems to meet silence?
Was God only faithful when life was comfortable?
Or have we confused His faithfulness with our preferred outcomes?
That question hurts.
Especially when you have obeyed God through tears, served Him through exhaustion, and watched someone else receive the very thing you have been begging Him for.
There is a particular kind of spiritual pain that comes when you know the right Bible verses but cannot understand your own life.
You know Romans 8:28.
You know Jeremiah 29:11.
You know that God is good.
Yet your heart still aches.
And sometimes you feel guilty for hurting because you think genuine Christians should be stronger than this.
But Lamentations gives us a different picture.
The Bible does not demand that grieving believers pretend they are happy.
It gives them words for their grief.
It allows lament.
It allows tears.
It allows anguished questions to be brought before the living God.
Faith does not always sound like a victorious shout.
Sometimes faith sounds like a broken whisper:
Lord, I do not understand what You are doing. But I know You have not stopped being who You are.
And that is not weak faith.
That is faith learning to rest on God's character rather than the appearance of immediate circumstances.
But there is something else we need to understand.
The suffering described in Lamentations had a particular historical and covenant context. Jerusalem's destruction was connected to Judah's rebellion and God's announced judgment.
That does not mean every tragedy in your life is punishment for a specific sin.
Scripture itself rejects that simplistic assumption.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus challenged the idea that a man's blindness must have resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
And in Luke 13:1–5, Jesus refused to portray victims of tragedy as worse sinners than everyone else.
So please do not turn Lamentations into a weapon against every hurting person.
A grieving mother does not need someone casually telling her that her loss must be God's punishment.
A struggling believer does not need every hardship interpreted as evidence that God is angry.
Sometimes suffering exposes our sin and calls us to repentance.
Sometimes suffering comes through the evil actions of others.
Sometimes it reflects the brokenness of a fallen world.
And sometimes we simply do not know why God has permitted a particular trial.
But in every circumstance, we are invited to bring our pain honestly before Him.
Because biblical hope is not built on pretending we know every reason.
It is built on knowing the God who remains faithful.
And this brings us to a line that is often overlooked.
“The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him.”
— Lamentations 3:24 (KJV)
My portion.
Not my possessions.
Not my reputation.
Not my perfect future.
Not even the immediate restoration of everything I have lost.
The LORD Himself is my portion.
Can you feel the weight of that confession?
When almost everything that once gave life stability has been stripped away, the writer remembers that God Himself remains the deepest inheritance of His people.
This does not make the losses insignificant.
It makes the Lord greater than what has been lost.
And that truth becomes even more breathtaking when we follow the story of Scripture toward Jesus Christ.
Because Jerusalem's destruction was not the final chapter of God's redemptive plan.
God preserved His people.
He brought exiles home.
He continued His covenant purposes.
And in the fullness of time, the promised Messiah came.
Jesus Christ.
Not a Savior who stood at a comfortable distance from human suffering.
Not a King who demanded that hurting people become emotionally presentable before approaching Him.
But the Son of God who entered our broken world.
He wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
He was betrayed by someone close to Him.
He was abandoned by His disciples.
He was mocked, scourged, and crucified.
And on the cross, He bore our sins, fulfilling the saving purpose of God.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5 (KJV)
That healing cannot be reduced to a guarantee that every believer will immediately recover from every disease or escape every earthly hardship.
The passage points fundamentally to the Servant's redemptive suffering, through which God brings reconciliation and restoration to sinners.
At Calvary, the faithfulness of God was revealed in a way that human imagination could never have invented.
The righteous Son suffered for the unrighteous.
The sinless Savior bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The One who had every right to condemn became the sacrifice through whom forgiveness is offered.
And then came the resurrection.
The stone was rolled away.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
The grave did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And now the Gospel announces something infinitely greater than the possibility of an easier life.
It announces reconciliation with God through the crucified and risen Savior.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
— Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
This is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes intensely personal.
Because the greatest scandal in your story may not be what someone did to you.
It may be what you have done and cannot undo.
The secret sin.
The compromise.
The lies.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The years of resisting God's voice.
The choices you would never want displayed before the people who respect you.
And perhaps you have wondered whether the Lord could still receive someone who knows the truth and has repeatedly walked away from it.
Listen carefully.
God's mercy is not permission to continue in rebellion.
Grace is not a disguise for unrepentant sin.
The Gospel does not tell us that our sin was never serious.
The cross tells us just how serious it was.
But the cross also reveals how extraordinary God's mercy is toward sinners who come to Christ in repentance and faith.
The same Jesus who said, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15) also declared:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37 (KJV)
Think about that.
You may be ashamed of what you have become.
You may be exhausted from fighting the same temptation.
You may be carrying years of spiritual regret.
But the invitation of Christ is not to clean yourself up so thoroughly that you no longer need a Savior.
It is to come to Him because you desperately do.
To confess.
To turn from sin.
To trust His finished work.
To receive the forgiveness you could never purchase through your own religious performance.
And to follow Him in the new life His grace makes possible.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
Not by promising that repentance will instantly repair every broken relationship.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new standing before God, a new direction for their lives, and a living hope that suffering cannot ultimately destroy.
This is why Lamentations 3:23 is so powerful.
It was not written by someone who could see every beautiful thing God would eventually do.
It was written from within a story that still hurt.
And yet the writer could say:
Not because every morning brings good news.
Not because every morning erases yesterday's grief.
Not because every morning guarantees an unexpected financial breakthrough, a restored marriage, or a miraculous recovery.
But because God's compassion is not exhausted by yesterday.
His faithfulness is not diminished by the darkness of the night.
And His people can seek Him again.
There may be someone reading this who has not prayed sincerely in weeks.
You have been angry.
Disappointed.
Perhaps even numb.
You have opened your Bible, stared at the page, and closed it because you could not bear another promise that seemed so far from your present reality.
And now you are wondering whether God is tired of you.
Whether you have disappointed Him too many times.
Whether your spiritual life has become too damaged to rebuild.
Remember what Lamentations says:
“The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.”
— Lamentations 3:25 (KJV)
And later:
“For the Lord will not cast off for ever: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies.”
— Lamentations 3:31–32 (KJV)
These words do not promise that every earthly situation will turn out as we wish.
They do reveal the compassion of the Lord within the covenant story of His people.
And through Jesus Christ, we have the assurance that everyone who belongs to Him has a hope extending beyond this present age.
The final restoration promised in Scripture is not merely a return to the life we used to have.
It is something greater.
A new heaven and a new earth.
God dwelling with His people.
Death abolished.
Mourning ended.
Sin removed.
And every tear finally wiped away.
Revelation 21:4 says:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.”
That is the future toward which Christian hope ultimately looks.
Not an endless cycle of earthly disappointments interrupted by occasional blessings.
But the final victory of Jesus Christ over sin, death, and all that has corrupted God's creation.
Until then, we walk by faith.
Sometimes with confidence.
Sometimes with trembling hands.
Sometimes singing.
Sometimes crying so hard that the only prayer we can manage is His name.
Jesus.
And that name is enough to begin praying again.
Maybe today you need to stop measuring God's faithfulness by how quickly your circumstances change.
Maybe you need to repent of a sin you have been protecting.
Maybe you need to surrender the bitterness that has slowly become part of your identity.
Maybe you need to forgive someone, even while establishing wise boundaries and acknowledging the damage they caused.
Maybe you need to ask for help because the weight you are carrying has become too heavy to bear alone.
Or maybe you simply need to hear this:
Your present ruins do not prove that God has abandoned you.
And your inability to understand His timing does not make His promises untrue.
There is a beautiful difference between saying, “I know everything will happen exactly as I want,” and saying, “I know the Lord is faithful, whatever happens.”
The first depends on an outcome.
The second depends on God.
And only one of those foundations can hold when the outcome breaks your heart.
Be honest before God.
Not as a performance.
Not because a public comment earns God's attention.
But because sometimes admitting that we need prayer becomes the first honest conversation we have had in a long time.
Let those words become your confession, not that everything is okay, but that the Lord remains worthy of your trust.
Perhaps someone else reading the comments needs to know they are not the only believer struggling to hold on.
And if you see someone asking for prayer, consider taking a moment to pray for them.
We were never meant to carry every burden alone.
That is also why I hope you will not keep this article to yourself.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because somewhere among your friends and family may be someone who is quietly losing hope.
Someone who has stopped attending church.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to Jesus.
Someone who is wondering whether God still sees them.
You may never know how much a Scripture-filled message means to a person who was barely holding on when they encountered it.
Because spiritual growth is not sustained by one emotional moment.
We need the Word of God repeatedly.
We need prayer.
We need fellowship with faithful believers.
We need sound teaching.
We need correction when we wander.
And above everything else, we need Jesus Christ.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.

We want to help people move beyond simply being inspired by Christian content toward actually knowing Scripture, growing in discernment, confronting sin, understanding grace, and following Jesus more faithfully.
These resources are intended to help believers become more deeply rooted in the Word of God, better equipped to face life's struggles, and more confident in sharing the Gospel.
And I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
It helps sustain a ministry committed to proclaiming Christ in a world where countless people are spiritually hungry.
But please understand something important.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not make anyone more spiritual than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you have toward your family, your local church, or people genuinely in need.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a beautiful expression of generosity and stewardship.
What matters is that your giving be voluntary, thoughtful, and offered with a sincere desire to honor the Lord.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful part of Christian generosity.
You may never hear the prayer they whisper.
You may never know which Bible passage finally helped them understand the Gospel.
But you can participate in helping the truth reach farther.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not a product.
Salvation is the gift of God, received through faith in the Savior.
Our desire is simply to make the truth of that Gospel known.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the person we met at the beginning.
The person standing in the ruins.
The person who has been trying to understand why life hurts so much.
The person who still believes in God but feels ashamed to admit how tired they are.
Perhaps that person is you.
I cannot promise that tomorrow will bring the answer you have been waiting for.
I cannot promise that everyone who left will return.
I cannot promise that your illness will disappear, that your finances will immediately recover, or that every broken relationship will be restored.
Scripture does not authorize me to make those promises.
But I can point you to the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
To the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
To the Lord whose mercy is not exhausted.
To the One who has promised never to forsake those who belong to Him.
And I can remind you that the book containing the words “Great is thy faithfulness” did not begin with a happy ending.
It began with a devastated city.
It contained mourning.
It contained confession.
It contained painful questions.
And right in the middle of it all, a wounded voice remembered the character of God.
Perhaps your circumstances have not changed yet.
Perhaps the tears are still there.
Perhaps you are still waiting.
But tonight, you can bring your honest heart before the Lord.
You do not need an impressive prayer.
You do not need to manufacture an emotion.
You can simply say:
Father, I am tired.
I have questions I cannot answer.
I have carried things I should have surrendered.
Forgive my sins. Cleanse my heart. Teach me to trust You.
Help me remember Your mercy when I cannot understand my circumstances.
Keep my eyes on Jesus, who died for sinners and rose again.
And when tomorrow comes, help me seek You again.
Amen.
There is no magic in repeating those words.
The hope is not in the prayer itself.
The hope is in the living God to whom we pray.
And if you have never truly turned to Jesus Christ, do not settle for being moved by an article.
Respond to the Gospel.
Repent and believe in Him.
Seek to know Him through His Word.
Become part of a faithful local church where you can be taught, encouraged, corrected, and loved.
Because the goal is not merely to feel stronger for a few minutes.
The goal is to belong to Christ and walk with Him for the rest of your life.
What has God's faithfulness taught you in a season you never wanted to experience?
You do not have to share anything too personal.
Even a simple “I'm still trusting Jesus” may encourage someone else to keep seeking Him.
The world often celebrates faith when the miracle arrives.
But Scripture also shows us faith that waits.
Faith that mourns.
Faith that repents.
Faith that remembers.
Faith that keeps turning toward the Lord when there is no visible reason to celebrate.
And maybe that is the testimony your life is becoming.
Not that you were never broken.
Not that you never struggled.
Not that you always understood.
But that, by the grace of God, you learned to look toward Jesus even through tears.
The ruins may still be standing around you, but they do not get to write the final sentence of the story Christ is redeeming.
